title: Managing Disappointment
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ISKY2Bgz_c0

Daniel (@dungeondive) sits down with Secrets of the Lost Station and makes a point of saying what this video is not: a negative review. He has stopped doing those — they are stressful, and the aftermath is a long defence of his own opinion against people who love the game. He also doesn't think this is a bad game. The rules are well written, the components are nice, and there are ninety-odd missions and hundreds of hours in the box.

What it isn't, for him, is a good sequel to Secrets of the Lost Tomb — his favourite game of all time. The analogy he reaches for is Star Trek: The Motion Picture released as the sequel to Star Wars: both good, wildly different, and presenting one as the follow-up to the other carries baggage. Five hours and several scenarios in, he isn't having fun, and the comparison is impossible to switch off when the box itself calls it a sequel.

The rest is about disappointment as a thing to manage rather than argue with. Kickstarter stacks money, time and emotion on a game before it arrives, which makes admitting disappointment expensive. His answer is to sell it: the house is small, the shelf is finite, and Lost Tomb still exists to be played.

----

Have you ever had to let go of a long-anticipated game, and did selling it make the disappointment easier?
